lessonRef.subject: ready-for-life
lessonRef.title: Guided practice: requests, declines, and boundaries

objective: Learners draft one request message asking an adult outside their household for something specific, and one polite-decline message turning down a request from a peer, each following a three-part template (state the situation, state the request or decline clearly, offer or ask about an alternative), so they can state a boundary respectfully without over-explaining or apologizing excessively.
scenario: The learner works from two short scenario prompts on this task sheet, one where they need to ask a coach or teacher for something specific, and one where a friend has asked them for something they need to turn down, and drafts both messages using the three-part template, without sending either message to anyone.
safetyNotes: Both messages drafted in this lesson are practice only; neither is sent to a real recipient, and no real contact information is needed to complete this task sheet.
materials: the three-part request/decline template on this task sheet

tasks.directions: Read the two scenarios below. Scenario 1 (request): You want to ask a coach or teacher if you can retake a quiz you did poorly on. Scenario 2 (decline): A friend has asked to copy your homework answers before class and you don't want to say yes.

prompts.text: For each scenario, write down what makes it uncomfortable to bring up, and what you actually want the outcome to be.

tasks.directions: Draft your request message for Scenario 1 using the three-part template: state the situation in one sentence, state exactly what you're asking for, then ask one specific follow-up question (such as a possible time).

prompts.text: My message states the situation in one sentence without over-explaining or apologizing more than once.
My message states exactly what I'm asking for in a single clear sentence.
My message ends with one specific follow-up question, such as offering a time or asking what would work.

tasks.directions: Draft your decline message for Scenario 2 using the three-part template: acknowledge the request, state your decline clearly in one sentence, then offer one honest alternative if one exists.

prompts.text: My decline states 'no' or an equivalent clear refusal in one sentence, not buried in apologies.
My decline does not blame a rule or a third party for the refusal — it states it as my own decision.
What honest alternative, if any, did you offer, and why is offering it different from changing your answer to yes?

tasks.directions: Compare how it felt to draft the request versus the decline.

prompts.text: Which message was harder to keep clear and boundaried without over-apologizing, and what specific sentence did you have to revise to fix that?

remediation: If a learner's decline message apologizes more than once or hedges with phrases like 'maybe' or 'I guess,' reteach by having them state the refusal alone as a single flat sentence first ('I'm not going to do that'), then add exactly one sentence of context before or after it, so the boundary itself stays unambiguous.
extension: Have the learner draft a third message declining a request from an adult outside their household, such as a coach asking them to take on an extra commitment, using the same three-part template and noting what changes when the recipient is an adult rather than a friend.
